question: When the author identifies the visible brain in the on-screen interviewee silhouette as the underlying model of language and finishes describing its ability to predict letters from context, state how this answers the earlier on-screen P[Language] ??? question: which source of next-letter probabilities Shannon turned to, and why that source avoids the problem that makes a corpus frequency table unusable.

triggers.response: The source is people, native speakers: Shannon asked a person to guess each next letter and reconstructed the probabilities from those guesses. That source has no sparsity problem because a person is not a table of frequencies but a model of the language: they give an estimate for a context they have never seen verbatim, generalising rather than looking for an exact match in a corpus. It is precisely on long context, where corpus statistics are empty, that predictability is highest and compression can go furthest.
rubric: it is named that the source was people (experiments on guessing the next letter)
it is named why corpus statistics are unusable: long n-grams are not in the corpus
it is named why a person is free of this: they generalise to a context never seen rather than looking for an exact match — that is, they work as a model of the language rather than as a table
do NOT count an answer that names only the source (“Shannon asked people”) without explaining how a person differs from a table of frequencies: that is half the answer
do NOT count a general answer “you need a language model” with no mention of people
